nameStory: The Red-fingered Coryphella gets its name from the vibrant red or orange tips on its finger-like projections called cerata (pronounced sir-AH-tah). These colorful 'fingers' look like tiny red-tipped paintbrushes sprouting from its back, giving this sea slug its memorable common name.
description: The Red-fingered Coryphella is a type of sea slug called a nudibranch, which means 'naked gill' because it breathes through exposed projections on its back. This soft-bodied marine creature has a translucent white or pale body decorated with numerous finger-like projections (cerata) that are tipped with bright red or orange. It's a small animal, typically measuring less than an inch long, and belongs to a group of sea slugs that are known for their striking beauty and alien-like appearance.

idTips.label: Red-tipped fingers
idTips.description: Look for numerous finger-like projections (cerata) extending from the back, each distinctively tipped with bright red or orange color that looks almost like nail polish

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: The main body appears glassy or translucent white, allowing you to sometimes see internal structures through the skin

idTips.label: Clustered cerata
idTips.description: The finger-like projections are arranged in distinct clusters along the back, creating a organized pattern rather than random placement

idTips.label: Two tentacle pairs
idTips.description: The head features two pairs of tentacles - longer ones at the back (rhinophores) and shorter oral tentacles near the mouth

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically less than an inch long, making it easy to overlook among seaweed and rocks in tide pools

habitat: Found in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal waters along New England's coast, particularly in areas with good water circulation. Look for them crawling on rocks, seaweed, or hiding under overhangs in tide pools during low tide. They prefer areas where their prey (small hydroids) are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Active and more visible as water temperatures begin to warm, often found in shallow tide pools during spring low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most commonly observed feeding and moving about in tide pools and shallow rocky areas.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin moving to slightly deeper waters as temperatures cool, though still findable in protected tide pools.
seasonality.winter: Less commonly seen as they retreat to deeper waters or more protected areas, though mild winter days may still offer sightings.

funFact: This sea slug is essentially a solar-powered predator - it eats tiny animals called hydroids and can actually steal and use the stinging cells from its prey, incorporating them into its own finger-like projections for defense!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small nudibranchs, but the distinctive red-tipped finger-like projections are unique. Remember: red fingertips = Red-fingered Coryphella. Other similar sea slugs either lack the bright red tips or have completely different body shapes.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gill' in Latin, referring to how these sea slugs breathe through exposed projections rather than hidden gills like most marine animals. Don't be fooled by their delicate appearance - these are active predators in the miniature world of tide pools.
compareHints: The Red-fingered Coryphella differs from its close relative the Slender Eolis by having distinctly red-tipped cerata, whereas the Slender Eolis typically has more uniform coloring without the bright red fingertips. The Red-fingered Coryphella also tends to have a more robust body shape compared to the aptly-named slender build of its cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest New England relative, the red-fingered coryphella, the slender eolis lives up to its name with a noticeably more elongated and delicate body form.
